newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook--Focus on downside, April pricing.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook--Focus on downside, April pricing.

text.p: Base metal markets this week will focus on the downside and Third Wednesday pricing after a bout of fund selling last week left the LME complex limping and the charts damaged, analysts said.
Volumes might gather momentum as players priced April contracts later on Monday, especially if prices slid to fresh lows, they added.

Key levels to watch on three months copper would be the $2,365 per tonne low touched last Monday when investment funds unleased an onslaught of selling, the 100-day moving average, which finished Friday at $2,359, and a technical support level at $2,340/50.

Copper hovered above the lows after Monday's losses, supported by steadily declining stocks, which were 14,800 tonnes down at the end of the first week of daily inventory reports. Monday's stocks declined by 1,775 tonnes.
But by Friday the market had lost confidence and ended the week $61 lower at $2,269.
"I can't see the funds dipping in again until the lows are violated, let's say $2,350 for copper," a senior trader said.
Waterside Futures has targeted a move to $2,215/17, a Fibonacci 61.8 percent retracement from copper's climb to $2,442 after the market failed to hold above the 38.2 percent support at $2,302.
Copper consumers gather in Japan this week for the annual meeting of the International Wrought Copper Council (IWCC), which opened on Sunday and winds up on Thursday.
Aluminium was also looking shaky after failing to break back through the $1,600 level and then dropping through the 100-day moving average.
This market, which saw more modest stock drawdowns than copper's at 6,775 tonnes, finished Friday's kerb $43 softer at $1,564, the low of the week.
Physical traders will be eyeing any further falls in futures to see if it sparks consumer buying.

"We had some very good business last Monday," said a trader in physical aluminium on continental Europe. But business tapered when the stronger dollar against the mark wiped out the advantage the following day, he added.
Lead ended last week with a $43 loss at $627 after hitting 18-month lows and giving off wobbly technical signals.
"Lead really does not look good. A test of $600 would not be beyond the realm of possibility," said analyst Helen Williamson of broker Brandeis.
Zinc had solid support at $1,220/25, but if that gave way a fall to $1,190 was on the cards, she added.
That lower level was the breakout area from mid-February where many people entered the market.
